$description: Every foreground/background combination Mizan intends to render, with the WCAG context each is used in. machinery/scripts/check-contrast.mjs resolves both tokens in every mode combination and fails the build when a declared pair falls below its threshold. An undeclared pairing is an unchecked pairing: nothing here means nothing verified, so coverage matters as much as strictness. The escape hatch is an explicit exception with a stated reason, never a lowered threshold — and an exception is reported in the build output whether it passes or fails, because a silent exception defeats the point of having a list. The context "decorative" is not an escape hatch but the absence of a claim: it says WCAG sets no bar for this pairing, so the ratio is reported and nothing is gated. It is legitimate only where 1.4.11 genuinely does not apply, and every use has to argue that in its own $description. See decisions/010-contrast-is-a-token-layer-guarantee.md.

pairs.$description: Body and heading text on the default surface. The most-used pairing in both products.
Body text inside a tinted panel. Sunken is lighter than the AA floor allows to be assumed, so it is checked separately from surface.default.
The second and last neutral text tier (decision 009). It resolves to a different value per product mode, so this pair is the one that proves the mode matrix rather than the base values.
Secondary text inside a tinted panel — the tightest neutral-on-neutral pairing in the system, and the first to break if either value drifts.

Label text on the primary action. action.primary resolves per product — green.600 in Market, blue.600 in Move (decision 008) — so this pair is two fills, not one, and both were set at the lightness that lets white sit on them: 5.64:1 on green.600 and 5.27:1 on blue.600. Theme never touches either, so the same two ratios hold in all four combinations. The blue is the binding case, and a brand change in either product has to clear 4.5 here before it ships.

The same label once the pointer is over it. A hover fill is a state of a control that is still being read, not a decoration, so it carries the full text threshold exactly as the resting state does. This pair was drawn in three places before it was declared anywhere — the preview's mode bar and both hover rules in the rebuilt pane — and it passed the whole time, at 8.09:1 on Market and 7.67:1 on Move, because the hover step goes darker under white. That is the argument for declaring it rather than against: it costs nothing today, and the day someone lightens a hover step to soften it, the gate is what notices. An undeclared pairing is an unchecked pairing whether or not it currently happens to pass.

FOCUS INDICATOR, THE TONE THAT MEETS THE FILL. The focus indicator is two-tone — a band of focus.ring with a band of focus.ring-contrast on either side of it — and this is the pairing that made it two-tone. A segmented control's buttons are flush, so an unpressed button's indicator is drawn across its pressed neighbour's fill, and the single focus.ring ring that used to be the whole indicator sat at 2.37:1 there. focus.ring-contrast is what meets that fill now, and it clears the 1.4.11 bar in every combination: 5.64:1 in light Market and 5.27:1 in light Move, where it is white, and 3.27:1 and 3.50:1 in dark, where it is neutral.1000. Dark Market is the binding case at 0.27 of headroom, and it is the number to watch if surface.default — the value focus.ring-contrast aliases — is ever lightened in dark. That tone is surface.default rather than text.on-action, which is white in both themes and would look like the safer choice at 5.64:1 either way: the other band is also white in dark, and an indicator whose two tones are the same colour is one tone.

FOCUS INDICATOR, THE OTHER TONE, drawn over the same neighbour's fill and never touching it. The focus.ring band sits between two bands of focus.ring-contrast, so what it is adjacent to is those, at 13.39:1. It is still painted over action.primary pixels, which is why it is declared rather than argued away: the pairing renders. Declared at the full 1.4.11 threshold and excepted in light rather than declared decorative or left out — decorative would be a false statement, since WCAG governs this indicator and this is part of it, and leaving it undeclared would hide the exact ratio the fix was made for. In dark it needs no exception at all: 5.64:1 on green.600 and 5.27:1 on blue.600, because focus.ring is neutral.0 there and the two tones have swapped which of them is the light one.

FOCUS INDICATOR, THE SAME TONE ON THE TINTED GROUND — the toolbar, the exhibit frames and the notes. 1.12:1 in all four combinations, and that is what a band in the page colour is supposed to do next to a panel one step off it: it disappears into it, and focus.ring at 11.96:1 / 16.48:1 is the whole indicator here. Declared and excepted on the same terms as focus.ring on action.primary. It is one of the six pairings two tones across three grounds can produce, and the six are accounted for rather than declared six times: three carry a focus name — this one and the two on action.primary; two are the same values already declared as text.primary on surface.default and text.primary on surface.sunken, which focus.ring aliases exactly and which are gated at 4.5 rather than 3.0, so the indicator case is covered by the stricter bar under the older name; and the sixth, focus.ring-contrast on surface.default, is a token against itself at 1.00:1 by construction rather than by measurement, which is the one that is not a pairing at all.

The 1px neutral hairline around a card, and the divider between list rows. Declared decorative, which means the ratio is measured and reported but nothing gates it. WCAG 1.4.11 governs the boundaries that identify user interface components and their states; a container hairline identifies no component and carries no state, so it is not one. Declaring it "ui" would be a category error with a visible cost — it would force every card border to roughly #949494 or darker, which is a boxed-in, heavily ruled interface nobody asked for. Leaving it undeclared would be worse: an undeclared pairing is an unchecked one, and this is the most-drawn line in either product. So it is declared, resolved in every mode, and printed on every run — visible to the system, and not wrongly failed by it. The moment a border starts identifying a control, it is border.control, and that one is gated.
The boundary of an interactive control. Checked separately from border.default because a control edge carries more meaning than a divider and may not inherit the same value.

The same control edge on the tinted ground — a field inside a card body, a control in a well. It renders today and was undeclared until decision 023: Button's own stylesheet draws border.control against surface.sunken and nothing checked the result, which is the plainest form of the hole this file exists to close. It passes, at 3.83:1 in light and 3.84:1 in dark against a 3.0 bar, and that it passes is the argument for declaring it rather than against — 0.83 of headroom on the tighter of the two grounds is the number somebody needs to see before nudging border.control a step lighter to soften a form.

The error message on the page ground. A sentence a user reads to find out what to fix, so it takes the full 4.5 text threshold and not the indicator one — this is the half of the invalid state that says what is wrong, and a message nobody can read is a control with no error state at all. red.600 in light and red.300 in dark, the ramp's own light-grounds/dark-grounds split.

The same message inside a tinted panel, which is where a form most often sits. Declared separately from surface.default for the reason every foreground in this file is: sunken is the tighter of the two grounds in both themes, so it is the binding case, and a red that reads on the page can still be the one that fails in the card the form lives in.

The edge of a control whose value was not accepted. Gated at 3.0 rather than the 4.5 its twin text.error carries, and that difference is the entire reason decision 023 made them two names for one value: a single name would have had to be declared at one threshold and would have been wrong at the other. An edge identifies a control and its state, which is precisely what 1.4.11 governs.

The invalid edge on the tinted ground, declared on the same terms as border.control on surface.sunken directly above — a form inside a card is the ordinary case, not the exotic one, and the invalid state has to survive the ground the form is actually drawn on.
Discount pricing is read as text and priced as a promise, so it carries the full 4.5 text threshold rather than the indicator threshold.
Trip cancellation and other destructive mobility messaging. Text, so 4.5. Kept distinct from commerce.discount by decision 008 — value coincidence is not semantic identity.

INDICATOR ONLY. Amber cannot reach 4.5 without becoming brown, so this token is a dot, bar or badge fill and must never carry text (decision 008). Any text beside the indicator uses text.primary. Checked at the 3.0 non-text threshold precisely because the text use is forbidden — if this pair is ever declared as context text, the token is being misused.
INDICATOR ONLY, on the same terms as commerce.stock.low. Surge pricing is signalled by a graphic element; the price itself is text.primary. Never text (decision 008).

exceptions.reason: The dark band of the two-tone focus indicator, drawn over a pressed neighbour's fill in the light theme: 2.37:1 in Market and 2.54:1 in Move, against a 3.0 bar. It is excepted because 1.4.11 asks for 3.0 from the indicator and not from each tone of it separately, and because this band does not touch the fill: it has a band of focus.ring-contrast on either side of it, at 13.39:1 against it and 5.64:1 / 5.27:1 against the fill. That flanking is the whole mechanism, and it is what the exception is conditional on. Scoped to light rather than left open, so that the dark combinations, where this same tone is the one at 5.64:1 and 5.27:1, are reported as the plain passes they are. The exception is void the moment the light bands stop being drawn on both sides — a single ring in focus.ring is the failure this replaced, and it would inherit an argument that no longer describes it.

The light bands of the two-tone focus indicator on the tinted ground: 1.12:1, in all four combinations, which is why this one is not scoped to a theme. The same argument as the dark band on action.primary and the other half of it — on this ground focus.ring is the tone doing the work, at 11.96:1 and 16.48:1, and focus.ring-contrast is a band that disappears into a panel one step off it. A two-tone indicator only earns its name because each tone is allowed to vanish somewhere; a pair of tones that both had to clear 3.0 on every ground would be a pair that could not exist. Declared so the ratio is printed rather than absent, excepted so that a number nobody needs to clear does not fail a build.
